how:
Data-driven population segments (Shreyas, Nov 15: replace the keyword role labels; groups and subgroups labelled with who they are, what
they likely say and who they likely vote for; keep recalibrating).

DATING: everything uses launches dated before the cut C and reads fetched before C (default: now). Re-run nightly; segments keep stable ids.
1. Groups (taste). People with >= MIN_UP upvotes on launches of the 730 days before C. Features = TF-IDF topic profile (L2) of
   the launches they upvoted (launch co-vote SVD factors were tried and dropped: they grouped people by active weeks, not taste). MiniBatchKMeans, K groups. People with 1..MIN_UP-1 upvotes are assigned to the nearest
   group by their topic profile (flag low_signal). People with no upvote in the window: group "not active in the last 180 days".
2. Subgroups (style, within each group). Standardised [ln(1+upvotes 30d), comment rate, made/hunted a launch, reviews+stacks, follows,
   role keywords (multi-hot; no headline/bio is its own column)]; KMeans with k = 2..4 by group size, each subgroup >= 20 people.
3. Descriptors (computed, aggregate only): size, activity, role mix, share commenting / making, topics by lift vs the whole population,
   products most upvoted (share of the group and lift), and up to 60 of the group's own comments (text matched by comment id from the
   launch-page dump, condensed by Gemini into themes, never quoted).
4. Names: Gemini 2.5 Flash names ALL groups in one comparative call (then each group's subgroups in one call) from the descriptors only,
   told that shared traits (developer / founder / AI) do not distinguish and names must differ; topic-lift fallback if the call fails.
   Stable ids: new centroids are matched to the previous run's (Hungarian, cosine); a matched group keeps its id and name unless its
   descriptors drift (top-10 lifted topics overlap < 5), then it is renamed.
5. Calibration (every run): cut C' = C - 7 days, refit groups on data before C', then for each launch dated in [C', C) with >= 20 held
   backers compare the backers' group mix with (a) the model mix (group sizes x each group's affinity for the launch's topics) and
   (b) the population mix (group shares of upvotes in the 30 days before C'). Metric = mean total-variation distance (lower is better), launch bootstrap. Also: per group, the upvote-rate
   lift on launches whose first topic is one of the group's top-5 lifted topics (does "votes_for" hold out of sample?). Appended to
   history so drift is visible.
Outputs: PRIVATE person -> group/subgroup (salted ids) gs://.../tmp/e5/private/segments/<C>.parquet; PUBLIC (aggregates, groups/subgroups
>= 20 people, no ids/usernames/headlines): results/web/segments/<C>.json and results/web/segments/latest.json; calibration history
results/web/segments/calibration_history.jsonl. Launch topics: warehouse (2026) + H25_SRC daily files (2025) when set.
    H25_SRC=<dir> python population_segments.py <store dir> <cf dir> <scratchpad> [--cut YYYY-MM-DD] [--k 12] [--no-upload] [--no-llm]
k_rule: top level 3-5 (Shreyas, Nov 15), chosen by held-out log-likelihood per vote; subgroups 3-5 only where they add held-out fit

groups.name: Product Evaluators
groups.who: These users have been on Product Hunt for a long time, have many followers, and are highly engaged with products, often providing detailed feedback and suggestions.
says: They provide detailed feedback on product functionality, user experience, and potential improvements.
They often compare new products to existing solutions or express concerns about pricing and trials.
They share personal anecdotes about how products impact their lives or work.
groups.votes_for: They upvote products related to Software Engineering, iOS, Sales, SaaS, and No-Code, often focusing on tools that enhance productivity and design.

calibration.note: upvote rate on last week's launches in this unit's top-5 topics vs its rate on other launches, relative to everyone else (1 = no signal); units fit on data up to 7 days earlier and matched by member overlap; holds = lift >= 1.2 with >= 10 such launches and >= 20 member votes

groups.name: Emerging Developers
groups.who: These are newer users, often students or developers, with a moderate number of upvotes and a high rate of commenting, indicating active engagement with the community.
says: They frequently ask technical questions about implementation, setup, and comparisons to other tools.
They often identify as makers or developers, sharing their own experiences and challenges in building products.
They express excitement for new concepts and launches, often congratulating makers.
groups.votes_for: They are interested in Development, APIs, GitHub, Productivity, and Open Source, particularly products that offer new ways to build and interact with technology.

subgroups.name: Founding Devs
subgroups.who: These users are highly engaged developers and founders, actively launching their own products and participating in discussions.
says: Introducing their own products and explaining their genesis.
Asking detailed questions about product features and future integrations.
Sharing personal experiences and frustrations that led to building solutions.
subgroups.votes_for: They upvote products across various tech domains, with a slight preference for Social Media, Sales, and SaaS tools.

subgroups.name: Technical Inquirers
subgroups.who: These users are highly curious about the technical implementation and scaling of products, with a strong focus on development and APIs.
says: Inquiring about technical specifics like latency, rate limits, and underlying architectures.
Asking about practical implications of features, such as data handling and integration methods.
Commenting on the cleverness of technical solutions and design choices.
subgroups.votes_for: They show strong interest in Development, API, and User Experience tools, with a notable lift for Custom Keyboards and Website Builders.

subgroups.name: Productivity Seekers
subgroups.who: These users are less active in upvoting but comment on products that promise to streamline workflows and enhance productivity, often from a marketer's perspective.
says: Discussing the practical benefits and time-saving aspects of new tools.
Suggesting feature improvements and potential integrations.
Expressing enthusiasm for clean UIs and intuitive user experiences.
subgroups.votes_for: They are interested in products related to Sales, Social Media, Marketing, and Productivity, often with a no-code angle.

subgroups.name: Open Source Contributors
subgroups.who: This segment consists of highly engaged student developers who actively build and contribute to open-source projects, often sharing their own creations.
says: Announcing their own open-source projects and seeking feedback.
Discussing technical challenges and solutions in software development.
Expressing appreciation for local-first and transparent tools.
subgroups.votes_for: They upvote products in Development, GitHub, Open Source, and Developer Tools, showing a strong preference for software engineering solutions.

subgroups.name: Student Dev Enthusiasts
subgroups.who: These are highly active student developers who upvote frequently and are interested in the practical application and comparison of new development tools.
says: Asking about comparisons to existing solutions and unique selling propositions.
Inquiring about platform compatibility and export features.
Discussing the potential for new tools in personal projects and team workflows.
subgroups.votes_for: They are drawn to products in Development, Open Source, Mac, and GitHub, with a particular interest in tools that enhance productivity and design.

calibration.note: upvote rate on last week's launches in this unit's top-5 topics vs its rate on other launches, relative to everyone else (1 = no signal); units fit on data up to 7 days earlier and matched by member overlap; holds = lift >= 1.2 with >= 10 such launches and >= 20 member votes

groups.name: Curious Observers
groups.who: This large group of users is relatively new to Product Hunt, has few upvotes or followers, and often lacks complete profile information, suggesting a more passive engagement.
says: They express curiosity about how products work and their core functionalities.
They often ask about specific features, platform compatibility (e.g., iOS release), or open-source availability.
They share initial impressions, often positive, and express interest in trying out new tools.
groups.votes_for: They upvote products across various categories including Vibe coding, Development, Social Media, Design Tools, and Productivity, showing a broad interest in new software.

subgroups.name: Aspiring Makers
subgroups.who: This segment consists of relatively new users with moderate engagement, a significant portion of whom have launched or hunted a product, and many lack complete profile information.
says: They introduce their own products, explaining the problem they solve and their motivation for building them.
They ask practical questions about product functionality, implementation details, and potential use cases.
They share their personal experiences and frustrations that led them to create or appreciate a product.
subgroups.votes_for: They show a strong interest in developer tools, software engineering, and productivity applications, particularly those related to iOS, Mac, and open source projects.

subgroups.name: Curious Students
subgroups.who: This is the largest segment, characterized by very low engagement, a high percentage of incomplete profiles, and a strong representation of students.
says: They express general interest and follow product developments, often asking about language support or specific features.
They share positive feedback and excitement about new tools, especially those integrating AI into workflows.
They inquire about practical applications and how products can solve their specific problems, often related to note-taking or organization.
subgroups.votes_for: They are interested in development, no-code solutions, and productivity tools, with a notable lean towards social media and video-related products.

subgroups.name: Visual & No-Code Enthusiasts
subgroups.who: This segment has very low engagement, a high proportion of incomplete profiles, and a strong interest in visual and no-code tools, with a notable student presence.
says: They provide feedback on product performance and quality, sometimes expressing dissatisfaction or requesting refunds.
They ask about specific technical capabilities, such as language support, water resistance, or integration with other platforms.
They inquire about pricing models and potential discounts for early adopters or teams.
subgroups.votes_for: They are highly interested in art, business intelligence, email marketing, bots, and website builders, with a significant focus on no-code and visual creation tools.

subgroups.name: Data & Marketing Reviewers
subgroups.who: This segment has low engagement but a high rate of reviewing products, with well-completed profiles and a strong representation of marketers and designers.
says: They provide detailed feedback on product design, functionality, and user experience, often suggesting improvements.
They discuss the underlying technology and architecture of products, particularly concerning AI agents and data processing.
They share personal use cases and how products fit into their workflows, often highlighting efficiency gains.
subgroups.votes_for: They show a strong preference for products related to data, search, advertising, and marketing, including Chrome extensions and design tools.

calibration.note: upvote rate on last week's launches in this unit's top-5 topics vs its rate on other launches, relative to everyone else (1 = no signal); units fit on data up to 7 days earlier and matched by member overlap; holds = lift >= 1.2 with >= 10 such launches and >= 20 member votes

groups.name: Launch Veterans
groups.who: These highly active users have a significant number of lifetime upvotes, followers, and products launched, indicating deep involvement in the product development and launch ecosystem.
says: They frequently identify as makers, founders, or hunters, sharing their personal experiences in building and launching products.
They offer detailed insights into product use cases, challenges, and potential improvements, often from a builder's perspective.
They engage in discussions about product strategy, pricing, and market positioning.
groups.votes_for: They are interested in SaaS, Marketing, Sales, Design Tools, and No-Code, often focusing on tools that support product development, marketing, and business growth.

subgroups.name: Product Launchers
subgroups.who: These users are highly engaged, frequently commenting and launching products, with strong representation from founders, designers, and developers.
says: Expressing excitement and congratulations for new launches.
Sharing their own product launch announcements and development journeys.
Discussing specific features, problems solved, and technical aspects of products.
subgroups.votes_for: They upvote products in SaaS, Marketing, Design Tools, Sales, and No-Code, often focusing on tools that enhance product development and business operations.

subgroups.name: Community Engagers
subgroups.who: These users are very active in commenting and have a high rate of launching products, with a notable presence of founders and investors.
says: Offering congratulations and positive feedback on launches.
Sharing their own product's development and problem-solving approach.
Discussing the practical applications and potential use cases of new tools.
subgroups.votes_for: They show interest in iOS, Software Engineering, Sales, SaaS, and No-Code products, often those that address business challenges or offer innovative solutions.

subgroups.name: Influential Reviewers
subgroups.who: These users are highly active in commenting and reviewing products, with significant representation from investors, marketers, product managers, and founders.
says: Congratulating teams and wishing them luck on their launches.
Sharing their personal experiences and motivations behind building products.
Discussing the real-world problems new products aim to solve and their potential impact.
subgroups.votes_for: They upvote products in Sales, iOS, No-Code, SaaS, and Marketing, often focusing on tools that improve business processes, personal organization, and user experience.

subgroups.name: Developer Advocates
subgroups.who: These users are highly engaged in commenting and launching products, with a strong emphasis on developers and founders, and a high likelihood of having a GitHub link.
says: Explaining the problems their own products solve and their development journey.
Discussing technical aspects, open-source initiatives, and developer tools.
Expressing appreciation for innovative solutions and efficient workflows.
subgroups.votes_for: They are particularly interested in Open Source, GitHub, Development, Mac, and Software Engineering products, especially those that enhance coding, automation, and productivity for developers.

subgroups.name: Seasoned Curators
subgroups.who: These users have a high number of lifetime upvotes and followers, indicating long-term engagement, with a strong presence of investors, product managers, and founders.
says: Praising product simplicity and effectiveness in solving real problems.
Discussing the challenges of product development and team collaboration.
Sharing personal experiences and insights related to the product's domain.
subgroups.votes_for: They upvote products related to Mac, Video, Design Tools, Tech, and Software Engineering, often focusing on tools that streamline creative processes, improve team efficiency, and offer innovative interfaces.

calibration.note: upvote rate on last week's launches in this unit's top-5 topics vs its rate on other launches, relative to everyone else (1 = no signal); units fit on data up to 7 days earlier and matched by member overlap; holds = lift >= 1.2 with >= 10 such launches and >= 20 member votes

groups.name: Tech Innovators
groups.who: These users are highly engaged with a high number of upvotes, followers, and products launched, often identifying as developers, marketers, or product managers, and are keen on cutting-edge tech.
says: They discuss technical aspects of products, such as API usage, infrastructure, and integration capabilities.
They often inquire about pricing models, scalability, and how products differentiate from competitors.
They share personal experiences and use cases, often from a professional or technical standpoint.
groups.votes_for: They upvote products related to Mac, Developer Tools, GitHub, Tech, and Open Source, with a strong interest in innovative solutions and infrastructure.

subgroups.name: Product & Dev Launchers
subgroups.who: These users are highly active in launching products, often identifying as developers or product managers, and show strong engagement with developer tools and SaaS.
says: They frequently introduce their own products, explaining the problem they solve and their development journey.
They ask detailed technical questions about integrations, features, and underlying technologies.
They appreciate simplicity and lightweight solutions, often comparing new tools to existing ones.
subgroups.votes_for: They upvote products in Sales, SaaS, Social Media, Marketing, Video, and API categories, with a particular interest in Developer Tools.

subgroups.name: Connected Product Makers
subgroups.who: This segment consists of highly connected individuals, often founders, marketers, or developers, who are very active in commenting and launching products, with a strong online presence.
says: They frequently share their personal experiences and motivations behind building their products.
They engage in discussions about product design, user experience, and the practical application of new technologies.
They offer encouragement and congratulations to other makers, often highlighting specific features they appreciate.
subgroups.votes_for: They support launches in SaaS, No-Code, Design Tools, Education, Sales, and Marketing, showing a preference for products that enhance productivity and creativity.

subgroups.name: Tool Evaluators
subgroups.who: These users are relatively new to the platform, primarily upvoting rather than launching, and are interested in practical applications of new tools, often as product managers or marketers.
says: They frequently inquire about pricing, value proposition, and specific use cases to determine if a product is 'worth paying for'.
They ask about integrations and compatibility with existing workflows and platforms.
They express interest in how tools can simplify complex tasks and automate processes.
subgroups.votes_for: They favor products in Chrome Extensions, Design Tools, No-Code, Education, Social Media, and Productivity, focusing on tools that offer immediate utility.

subgroups.name: Mac & Dev Enthusiasts
subgroups.who: This segment is characterized by recent high activity, particularly in upvoting, and a strong interest in developer tools, open source, and Mac-specific applications, often identifying as developers or marketers.
says: They ask detailed questions about technical implementation, collaboration features, and scalability.
They share practical tips and creative uses for the products, often relating to personal productivity or workflow improvements.
They express a desire for Mac alternatives or specific platform support for new tools.
subgroups.votes_for: They are keen on products related to Mac, Developer Tools, GitHub, Open Source, and APIs, with a notable interest in software engineering solutions.

calibration.note: upvote rate on last week's launches in this unit's top-5 topics vs its rate on other launches, relative to everyone else (1 = no signal); units fit on data up to 7 days earlier and matched by member overlap; holds = lift >= 1.2 with >= 10 such launches and >= 20 member votes

accuracy_label: Segments: 5 top-level groups of all held Product Hunt users by KIND of user (activity, making, followers, curation, links, comments, taste), k chosen in 3-5 by held-out fit, with 3-5 subgroups only where they add held-out fit; every unit >= 20 people; names and 'says' are Gemini summaries of measured statistics and members' own past comments (paraphrased). PLAIN CALIBRATION: at the group level these segments do NOT predict which launches people vote for better than 'everyone votes like the average' (last week's 59 launches: group-mix distance 0.069 vs 0.068 for the population mix, paired [0.001, -0.0, 0.002]); 'votes for' held out of sample for 1 of 5 groups and 3 of 19 subgroups (votes_for_holds flags). Per launch, expected-voter mix vs base (leave-one-day-out, Nov 8-12): groups -0.011 [-0.026, +0.008] (not better), subgroups -0.063 [-0.086, -0.041] (better); the earlier 12-group version scored -0.054 [-0.075, -0.032] - the 3-5 grouping (Shreyas, Nov 15) trades that predictive edge for readability.
